title: Reaping What Israel Planted
overview: Hosea warns that Israel's wealth fed empty worship, broken promises and trust in military power, and that all of it will be swept away, while still urging the people to turn back to the LORD.

parts.label: Prosperity fed more altars (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The richer Israel's land grew, the more altars it built and the more lavishly it decorated its sacred standing stones, so its good harvests went into showy worship. Their hearts were divided, and the LORD says he will tear those altars and stones down.

parts.label: Kings and promises fail (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: Israel went through a rapid string of kings, several of them murdered, and the people admit that no king can help them once they have stopped honoring the LORD. Their oaths and treaties are empty words, so lawsuits sprout like poisonous weeds in a field meant for food.

parts.label: Calf, king and altars gone (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: Hosea mockingly renames Bethel ("house of God") as Beth Aven ("house of wickedness"), and its prized calf idol will be hauled to Assyria as tribute. Samaria's king will vanish like something light carried off on water (the Hebrew word is uncertain, so some translations say a twig and others say foam), weeds will cover the altars, and people will beg the hills to fall on them, words Jesus later echoes in Luke 23:30.

parts.label: Remembering Gibeah (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: Gibeah recalls the horrific rape and killing of a woman in Judges 19 to 21, which led to civil war. The Hebrew here is hard, so it may mean Israel has stayed in that kind of sin ever since, or that the people "stood their ground" and survived back then, but either way the LORD says nations will now gather to bind them for a "double sin" whose exact meaning scholars debate.

parts.label: From easy work to plowing (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: Israel is pictured as a young cow that enjoyed easy threshing work, where it could eat as it walked, but it will now be yoked for hard plowing, a picture of forced service under a foreign power. Keeping the farm picture, Hosea urges them to sow right living, reap steady love and break up their hardened ground, but they planted wrongdoing and trusted their own warriors instead.

parts.label: War reaches the fortresses (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Their forts will fall as brutally as when Shalman destroyed Beth Arbel, killing mothers along with their children, though scholars are unsure who Shalman was (possibly the Assyrian king Shalmaneser) or which battle this was. Bethel, the center of their worship, becomes the cause of their ruin, and the king will be cut off as suddenly as dawn breaks.

think: What do people tend to rely on when life is going well, and does that change when things fall apart?
